blocks.text: BC Turkey Farms: streets and boundaries

items.t: This is a provincial page: the BC Turkey Marketing Board regulates the production of all turkey grown for meat or eggs in British Columbia.
The Board's office is in Cloverdale, Surrey: British Columbia Turkey, Suite 106 – 19329 Enterprise Way, Surrey, per the Board's own page.

blocks.text: BC Turkey Farms: the housing stock

items.t: A turkey farm is a quota holding in kilograms, not a bird count: the national quota is set in live weight and allotted to registered producers, per BCFIRB's Sunrise decision.
The personal-use ceiling is small and specific: any entity growing more than the allotted 50 turkeys per year for personal consumption is subject to the Board's Order and Regulations.
The Board dates to 1966: before it, each farmer negotiated their own price and secured their own poults, with prices sometimes falling below the cost of raising turkeys.

blocks.text: BC Turkey Farms: rules that affect buyers

items.t: The Board licenses the whole chain: under the Natural Products Marketing (BC) Act and the BC Turkey Marketing Scheme it licenses turkey farmers, hatcheries and processors, sets the minimum live price in negotiations with processors, and maintains the quota system.
The Board is overseen by BCFIRB, the same supervisor as the egg board.

Quota transfers fund new entrants in turkey too: BCFIRB's 2009 letter records the Turkey Board moving to a direct 5 per cent transfer assessment, with exemptions for direct family members, businesses and partnerships.

The land under a turkey barn is usually Agricultural Land Reserve (ALR = Agricultural Land Reserve) land, with the ALR Use Regulation residence caps of 500 square metres (m²) principal and 90 m² additional.

blocks.text: BC Turkey Farms: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: Utilization is not always 100 per cent: BCFIRB's 2019 accountability summary records BC turkey producers used 85.6 per cent of their quota in the April 29, 2018 – April 27, 2019 period.

The transfer assessment changed method, not just rate: the Board's earlier deemed (pooled) assessment was replaced by a direct assessment on the transferor, with BCFIRB recording it had no objection to the change in 2009.
Price is negotiated, not posted by the farmer: the Board sets the minimum live price for turkey in negotiations with processors.
Normal farm practice protection covers turkey barns as farm businesses, through the BCFIRB farm practices complaint process.

blocks.text: BC Turkey Farms: development and new projects

items.t: Processor allocation framework, BCFIRB supervisory review of the Turkey Board: base processor shares set from the 2006/07 quota year. Status: supervisory decision issued January 26, 2006, supplemental decision March 21, 2006 (as of November 3, 2026).

blocks.text: BC Turkey Farms: costs and taxes

items.t: The transfer cost to budget is the assessment: a direct 5 per cent quota transfer assessment applies on turkey quota transfers, with exemptions for direct family members, businesses and partnerships, per BCFIRB's 2009 letter.
Birds move to allotted processors: the processor allocation system in BCFIRB's supervisory decisions is the route from farm to plant, not an open market.

blocks.text: BC Turkey Farms: risks and due diligence

items.t: Verify quota in kilograms and its processor allocation together: a quota holding without processing room was the subject of the Sunrise and Rossdown appeals decided by BCFIRB.
Verify the licence status of the whole chain for the operation: the Board licenses farmers, hatcheries and processors, so a gap at any stage affects the farm's route to market.

Verify the land separately from the quota: ALR status and municipal zoning are checked on the parcel through the Agricultural Land Commission (ALC = Agricultural Land Commission) process, not through the Turkey Board.

faq.q: What should I check about barn capacity before valuing a turkey operation?
faq.a: Verify the specific operation's position with the board and an inspector rather than from listing text.

faq.q: What is the ALR and does it apply to farms in BC?
faq.a: The Agricultural Land Reserve is farmland protected by the provincial Agricultural Land Commission. Farm use is generally allowed on ALR land, but subdividing, adding homes or using the land for non-farm purposes usually needs approval, so check a property's ALR status before you offer.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a farm in BC?
faq.a: Check the ALR status, water source and licences, drainage and flood history, the buildings and any quota or production licences that do or do not transfer with the land. Poultry and egg production in BC are supply-managed, so a sale of the farm does not automatically include quota.

faq.q: How do I find out which school serves an address in BC?
faq.a: School catchments are set by address, so use the school district's catchment locator with the exact address. Catchment lines change, so check before you write an offer.
